vignette:
She is 32, South Asian, single, and works as a nurse, and for the past several years her life has been organized around one night that splits everything into before and after. Before the disaster, she describes herself as steady, practical, and used to being the person others leaned on. She had chosen nursing because she liked being useful in crisis, and she had always believed that if something went wrong, she would know what to do.

The disaster begins as a normal shift and becomes, in her memory, a series of broken images and sounds. There is confusion, shouting, the sharp smell of smoke and dust, and the instant sense that the world has become unsafe in a way she cannot explain. She is thrown into emergency mode, moving because moving is the only thing that keeps her from freezing. She remembers trying to help patients while the building shakes and the lights fail, her hands working almost automatically even as her mind struggles to make sense of what is happening. In the hours that follow, she sees injuries she cannot erase from memory and hears cries that return to her at unexpected moments. She survives, but she does not feel intact.

In the weeks after, she keeps telling herself that she is strong, that nurses are trained for this, that if she can just stay busy she will settle down. Instead, her body seems to continue living in the disaster even when the danger is over. She startles at sudden noises, flinches at slammed doors, and finds her heart racing when she smells burning, hears sirens, or sees a crowd moving quickly. She sleeps badly, waking from vivid dreams in which she is back in the scene, searching for patients, trying to reach people before it is too late. Some mornings she wakes already tense, with her jaw clenched and her chest tight, as if her body has spent the night bracing for impact.

At work, she becomes hyperaware of exits, alarms, and the tone of other people's voices. She still performs well, and colleagues often describe her as composed, but inside she is constantly scanning for what could go wrong. A dropped tray, a code blue, a sudden argument in the hallway can pull her immediately back into the disaster in a way that feels almost physical. She can lose track of the present for a few seconds and then realize she is gripping the edge of a cart so hard her knuckles have gone white. She hates that this is happening, because she believes she should be able to contain it. When she cannot, she turns inward and criticizes herself for being weak, even though she would never speak that way to a patient.

She begins avoiding reminders in ways that shape her life quietly but profoundly. She takes longer routes to work to avoid the site where the disaster occurred. She no longer watches news coverage of emergencies, and she leaves the room if someone starts talking about explosions, riots, or mass injuries. She declines invitations to crowded places and feels embarrassed by how quickly her mood changes when she is trapped in a busy restaurant or a packed train. She has not dated in any sustained way since the event, telling herself she is too busy, but part of her also does not want anyone close enough to notice how often she disappears into silence.

Over time, her emotional world narrows. She says she still functions, but it takes more effort than anyone realizes. She feels detached from friends and family, as if they are living slightly behind glass. She used to be warm and talkative; now she answers questions politely and then goes quiet. She has less interest in things that once made her feel like herself, including music, visiting relatives, and cooking with her mother over video calls. When she is alone, she often sits in stillness and feels an odd mix of sadness, irritability, and emptiness, as though the disaster took something essential and left her with the job of pretending otherwise.

What stands out most is the persistent sense that the world is dangerous and that safety can vanish in an instant. Even on ordinary days, she expects catastrophe to arrive without warning. She can know, intellectually, that she is no longer there, and still her body reacts as if she is. She lives by routines now: checking locks, planning escape routes, sitting near doors, keeping her phone charged. She says she is tired in a way sleep does not fix. Yet she continues to show up for her shifts, continues to help patients, and continues to move through her days with a disciplined exterior that hides how much effort it takes to remain present.
